name: Mini-cut

lead: A mini-cut is a brief, aggressive cutting phase, often 2 to 6 weeks, used to lose a limited amount of fat and restore definition before returning to maintenance or a bulk.

Calories are cut more sharply than in a regular cut for a short time. A summary source says the early weight lost is mostly water and glycogen, with about 1 to 2 percent body fat reduction. The term is common in lifting communities; no clinical studies were found.

paras: Lifters run it between bulking phases when they have gained more fat than wanted, then go back to maintenance or a surplus. It applies the standard calorie-deficit approach over a short window.

The same summary lists a higher chance of muscle loss, fatigue and metabolic slowdown, and recommends more gradual rates for most people. Wikipedia notes larger deficits bring faster weight loss but greater risk of losing muscle.

angle.text: Lifters use mini-cuts of a few weeks to shed recent fat between bulking phases and bring definition back without a long diet. It applies the established calorie-deficit pathway; the 2 to 6 week format is lifter convention.

lead: A mini-cut is a short, aggressive cutting phase in which a lifter eats well below maintenance for a few weeks to shed fat, usually between longer bulking phases. The aim is to look leaner and more defined, and to reset body-fat levels so the next bulk can start from a lower point [1].

A Grokipedia summary describes mini-cuts as lasting about 2 to 6 weeks, with 4 to 6 weeks cited for non-competitors, using deficits of roughly 500 to 1,500 or more calories a day [1]. It says they typically produce around 4 to 8 pounds of weight loss, or 1 to 2 percent body fat, with much of the early loss being water and glycogen [1].

The same source lists higher risks of muscle loss, fatigue and metabolic slowdown than a gradual cut, notes that risk rises when protein is low or resistance training is deprioritized, and contrasts mini-cuts with a gentler rate of 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight per week [1]. Wikipedia notes that larger deficits cause faster weight loss but a greater risk of losing muscle [2]. No clinical studies on mini-cuts were found.

paras: Cutting is eating in a net negative energy balance to lose fat while preserving muscle [2]. A mini-cut compresses this into a shorter, steeper deficit, and is often placed between bulks so a lifter can stay lean enough to keep gaining muscle for longer [1].

A Grokipedia summary reports most early weight lost is water and glycogen, with modest fat reduction, and cites greater risks of muscle loss, fatigue, overtraining and metabolic slowdown [1]. It says keeping resistance training a priority and protein adequate limits muscle loss, and it advises doing mini-cuts with guidance from a qualified professional such as a registered dietitian, coach or physician [1].
The term is common in bodybuilding and lifting forums, where it sits alongside bulking and regular cutting as one of the phases lifters cycle through [1][2].
